implementation_notes: In a ZIO/doobie stack the service is a class whose methods return ZIO, its dependencies are provided through a ZLayer graph resolved at the edge of the program, and repository ports expose ConnectionIO values. ZIO.serviceWithZIO obtains the Transactor[Task] from the environment and transact(xa) interprets the composed ConnectionIO in one transaction. What replaces the classic structure is the environment type and the interpreter: injection is the layer graph, the unit of work is the transaction interpreter, and the service itself stays a plain class of effect descriptions.
pitfalls: Wrong move: run a repository call as a standalone ZIO effect outside the ConnectionIO program; failure: it uses another connection or transaction; instead: compose every database operation as ConnectionIO and interpret the whole program with one Transactor.

Wrong move: provide the same ZLayer graph independently at multiple call sites; failure: resourceful services can be constructed more than once; instead: build and share one layer at the application edge.

Wrong move: catchAll an error and return success inside the transaction effect; failure: the interpreter sees a successful effect and commits partial work; instead: re-fail expected errors after logging or map them to a failed result.

variants.name: Plain OO service class with constructor-injected traits and manual JDBC demarcation
variants.idiom_name: final class with trait dependencies + setAutoCommit(false)/commit/rollback
variants.implementation_notes: The framework-free realization: a final class taking its ports as constructor parameters (traits), instantiated once at the composition root (manually, with MacWire or a Cake-style module); the transaction is demarcated explicitly on a JDBC connection with setAutoCommit(false), commit and a rollback in the catch, all in a try/finally that closes the connection. Choose it where the team wants neither an effect system nor a DI framework: everything is ordinary Scala, and the boundary is visible in the method body.
pitfalls: A rollback that itself throws in the catch clause masks the original failure; log and preserve the first error.
Passing java.sql.Connection through service signatures leaks JDBC into the domain; narrow it behind a transactor trait once more than one service needs it.
Blocking JDBC inside a Future without a dedicated execution context starves the global pool.
